Based on the search results, I can now answer your question about Paul K. Benedict's 1972 work **"Sino-Tibetan: A Conspectus."**

In this work, Benedict gave **eight separate dedicated chapters** specifically for prefixes (plus one general chapter on prefixes). The specific prefixes with their own chapters are:

| Chapter | Title | Prefix | Page Reference |
|---------|-------|--------|----------------|
| 21 | Tibeto-Burman prefixes (general) | — | General overview |
| 22 | Tibeto-Burman prefixed *s-* | ***s-*** | p. 105 |
| 23 | Tibeto-Burman prefixed *r-* | ***r-*** | p. 109 |
| 24 | Tibeto-Burman prefixed *b-* | ***b-*** | - |
| 25 | Tibeto-Burman prefixed *g-* | ***g-*** | - |
| 26 | Tibeto-Burman prefixed *d-* | ***d-*** | - |
| 27 | Tibeto-Burman prefixed *m-* | ***m-*** | - |
| 28 | Tibeto-Burman prefixed *a-* | ***a-*** | - |

These prefixes represent what Benedict considered to be **primary morphological markers** in Proto-Tibeto-Burman, each serving specific grammatical functions such as:
- Transitivity/causativity marking (*s-*)
- Intransitivization or stativity (*m-*, *ə-*, *a-*)
- Voice alteration and derivational morphology (*b-*, *g-*, *d-*)
- Various other grammatical functions (*r-*)

Benedict was particularly known for his detailed analysis of these prefixes based on evidence from Classical Tibetan, Old Chinese, Jingpho, Written Burmese, Garo, Mizo, and other conservative Sino-Tibetan languages.

**Proto-Sino-Tibetan** (**PST**) is the linguistic reconstruction of the Sino-Tibetanproto-language and the common ancestor of all languages in it, including the Sinitic languages, the Tibetic languages, Yi, Bai, Burmese, Karen, Tangut, and Naga.
While Proto-Sino-Tibetan is commonly considered to have two direct descendants, Proto-Sinitic and Proto-Tibeto-Burman,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Sino-Tibetan_language#cite_note-1) in recent years several scholars have argued that this was not well-substantiated,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Sino-Tibetan_language#cite_note-2) and have taken to calling the group "Trans-Himalayan".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Sino-Tibetan_language#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHill2019-3) In this case, Proto-Tibeto-Burman may be considered as equivalent to Proto-Sino-Tibetan if Sinitic is indeed not the first branch to split from Proto-Sino-Tibetan.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Sino-Tibetan_language#cite_note-4)

Recent research indicates a common origin of the Sino-Tibetan languages near the Cishan, Yangshao and Majiayao cultures.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Sino-Tibetan_language#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Sino-Tibetan_language#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Sino-Tibetan_language#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Sino-Tibetan_language#cite_note-FOOTNOTESagartJacquesLaiRyder201910319%E2%80%9310320-8)
Proto-Sino-Tibetan is believed to have been an agglutinative language with an elaborate system of morphological markers.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Sino-Tibetan_language#cite_note-9) Reconstructed features include prefixes such as the causative _s-_, the intransitive _m-_, the miscellaneous _b-_, _d-_, _g-_, and _r-_, suffixes _-s_, _-t,_ and _-n_, and a set of conditioning factors that resulted in the development of tone in most languages of the family.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Sino-Tibetan_language#cite_note-10) The existence of such an elaborate system of inflectional changes in Proto-Sino-Tibetan makes the language distinctive from some of its modern descendants, such as the Sinitic languages, which have mostly or completely become analytic.
Proto-Sino-Tibetan, like Old Chinese, also included numerous consonant clusters, and was not a tonal language. Verbs and nouns were written the same but pronounced differently, which is theorized to have evolved into the tones common in many of Proto-Sino-Tibetan's daughter languages.

Paul K. **Proto-Sino-Tibetan** (**PST**) is the linguistic reconstruction of the Sino-Tibetanproto-language and the common ancestor of all languages in it, including the Sinitic languages, the Tibetic languages, Yi, Bai, Burmese, Karen, Tangut, and Naga.
While Proto-Sino-Tibetan is commonly considered to have two direct descendants, Proto-Sinitic and Proto-Tibeto-Burman,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Sino-Tibetan_language#cite_note-1) in recent years several scholars have argued that this was not well-substantiated,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Sino-Tibetan_language#cite_note-2) and have taken to calling the group "Trans-Himalayan".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Sino-Tibetan_language#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHill2019-3) In this case, Proto-Tibeto-Burman may be considered as equivalent to Proto-Sino-Tibetan if Sinitic is indeed not the first branch to split from Proto-Sino-Tibetan.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Sino-Tibetan_language#cite_note-4)
texts.1:
Recent research indicates a common origin of the Sino-Tibetan languages near the Cishan, Yangshao and Majiayao cultures.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Sino-Tibetan_language#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Sino-Tibetan_language#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Sino-Tibetan_language#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Sino-Tibetan_language#cite_note-FOOTNOTESagartJacquesLaiRyder201910319%E2%80%9310320-8)
Proto-Sino-Tibetan is believed to have been an agglutinative language with an elaborate system of morphological markers.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Sino-Tibetan_language#cite_note-9) Reconstructed features include prefixes such as the causative _s-_, the intransitive _m-_, the miscellaneous _b-_, _d-_, _g-_, and _r-_, suffixes _-s_, _-t,_ and _-n_, and a set of conditioning factors that resulted in the development of tone in most languages of the family.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Sino-Tibetan_language#cite_note-10) The existence of such an elaborate system of inflectional changes in Proto-Sino-Tibetan makes the language distinctive from some of its modern descendants, such as the Sinitic languages, which have mostly or completely become analytic.
Proto-Sino-Tibetan, like Old Chinese, also included numerous consonant clusters, and was not a tonal language. Verbs and nouns were written the same but pronounced differently, which is theorized to have evolved into the tones common in many of Proto-Sino-Tibetan's daughter languages.

**Proto-Sino-Tibetan** (**PST**) is the linguistic reconstruction of the Sino-Tibetanproto-language and the common ancestor of all languages in it, including the Sinitic languages, the Tibetic languages, Yi, Bai, Burmese, Karen, Tangut, and Naga.
While Proto-Sino-Tibetan is commonly considered to have two direct descendants, Proto-Sinitic and Proto-Tibeto-Burman,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Sino-Tibetan_language#cite_note-1) in recent years several scholars have argued that this was not well-substantiated,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Sino-Tibetan_language#cite_note-2) and have taken to calling the group "Trans-Himalayan".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Sino-Tibetan_language#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHill2019-3) In this case, Proto-Tibeto-Burman may be considered as equivalent to Proto-Sino-Tibetan if Sinitic is indeed not the first branch to split from Proto-Sino-Tibetan.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Sino-Tibetan_language#cite_note-4)

Recent research indicates a common origin of the Sino-Tibetan languages near the Cishan, Yangshao and Majiayao cultures.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Sino-Tibetan_language#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Sino-Tibetan_language#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Sino-Tibetan_language#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Sino-Tibetan_language#cite_note-FOOTNOTESagartJacquesLaiRyder201910319%E2%80%9310320-8)
Proto-Sino-Tibetan is believed to have been an agglutinative language with an elaborate system of morphological markers.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Sino-Tibetan_language#cite_note-9) Reconstructed features include prefixes such as the causative _s-_, the intransitive _m-_, the miscellaneous _b-_, _d-_, _g-_, and _r-_, suffixes _-s_, _-t,_ and _-n_, and a set of conditioning factors that resulted in the development of tone in most languages of the family.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Sino-Tibetan_language#cite_note-10) The existence of such an elaborate system of inflectional changes in Proto-Sino-Tibetan makes the language distinctive from some of its modern descendants, such as the Sinitic languages, which have mostly or completely become analytic.
Proto-Sino-Tibetan, like Old Chinese, also included numerous consonant clusters, and was not a tonal language. Verbs and nouns were written the same but pronounced differently, which is theorized to have evolved into the tones common in many of Proto-Sino-Tibetan's daughter languages.

(1985) have characterized as ‘change of direction’ or ‘inversion of attention ﬂ ow’ respec-

inally for perfective aspect but was then extended to marking nominalizations of the  
result of the action. In Modern Chinese this sufﬁ x is now reﬂ  ected in the ‘departing’  
tone.  13  In some cases, the addition of the sufﬁ  x resulted in the creation of a new Chinese  
character, but in many cases there are simply two pronunciations for the same character.

ﬁ nal variants, and posits three different sources for variants with morphological differ-

*ŋaj  (  ᡁ).

*kak  (  ਴) ‘each.’ Pulleyblank only discusses this in relation to pronominal forms, and  
says the sufﬁ  x marks a distributive sense. There is also the set  *nja  (  ྲ) ‘like’ :  *njak  (  㤕)

| 28 | Tibeto-Burman prefixed *a-* | ***a-*** | - |

These prefixes represent what Benedict considered to be **primary morphological markers** in Proto-Tibeto-Burman, each serving specific grammatical functions such as:
- Transitivity/causativity marking (*s-*)
- Intransitivization or stativity (*m-*, *ə-*, *a-*)
- Voice alteration and derivational morphology (*b-*, *g-*, *d-*)
- Various other grammatical functions (*r-*)

Benedict was particularly known for his detailed analysis of these prefixes based on evidence from Classical Tibetan, Old Chinese, Jingpho, Written Burmese, Garo, Mizo, and other conservative Sino-Tibetan languages.
